blocks.text: 1. Apriori Algorithm

blocks.alt: Transactions produce frequent itemsets, which become association rules

blocks.text: The Clustering Algorithms module, just completed, asked one specific unsupervised question repeatedly: given unlabeled data, which data points naturally belong together? Association Rule Learning, the module this topic opens, asks a genuinely different unsupervised question. Rather than grouping similar data points, it looks at transactions, collections of items that occurred together, and asks which items tend to show up together far more often than random chance alone would predict.

Apriori is the classic, foundational algorithm for answering this exact question, and it remains the natural starting point for understanding the entire field of association rule mining. Given a large collection of transactions, Apriori systematically discovers which combinations of items appear together frequently enough to be worth paying attention to, forming the basis for everything from retail shelf placement decisions to online frequently-bought-together recommendations.
2. Market Basket Analysis

blocks.alt: Bread and butter are bought together often

blocks.text: The classic setting for Apriori, and the one that gives the field much of its vocabulary, is a retail store's transaction records. Every single transaction is treated as a basket, the complete set of items one customer purchased together in a single visit. Across thousands or millions of such baskets, the goal is to find itemsets, combinations of items, that appear together across many baskets meaningfully more often than would be expected if items were purchased independently of one another.

A classic illustrative discovery might be that customers who buy bread and butter also frequently buy jam in the same transaction, a pattern a retailer could act on directly, whether by placing jam near the bread and butter aisle, or by bundling the three items into a promotional offer. This entire practice is called Market Basket Analysis, and while retail is its namesake and most classic application, the same underlying technique applies to any dataset made up of transactions, sets of items occurring together.
3. Itemsets and Frequency

An itemset is simply any set of one or more items being considered together. A 1-itemset contains a single item, such as bread on its own. A 2-itemset contains a pair of items, such as bread and butter together. Larger itemsets, 3-itemsets and beyond, contain correspondingly larger combinations. Apriori works by systematically discovering which of these itemsets, across every possible size, actually appear together often enough in the transaction data to be considered frequent.

An itemset is called frequent if it appears together in at least some minimum fraction of all transactions, a threshold chosen by whoever is running the analysis, called minimum support, covered in far more depth in its own dedicated Support topic later in this module. Apriori's entire job, at its core, is to efficiently find every itemset, of every size, that clears this frequency bar, without having to individually check every single possible combination of items, a number that would explode combinatorially even for a modest catalog of products.
4. The Apriori Property

blocks.alt: An infrequent itemset means all its supersets are also infrequent

blocks.text: The insight that makes Apriori's search efficient, and gives the algorithm its name, is called the Apriori Property, also known as anti-monotonicity. It states a simple but powerful fact: if a particular itemset is infrequent, meaning it fails to meet the minimum support threshold, then every larger itemset that contains it as a subset must also necessarily be infrequent. Equivalently, stated the other way around, every subset of a genuinely frequent itemset must itself also be frequent.

This single property lets Apriori prune enormous portions of the search space without ever having to actually count them in the transaction data. If a 2-itemset like bread and caviar turns out to be infrequent, there is no need to even check any 3-itemset that contains both bread and caviar together, such as bread, caviar, and butter, since it is mathematically guaranteed to be infrequent too. This pruning is what separates Apriori from a brute-force approach that would need to check every conceivable combination directly.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The Apriori Property works in both directions as a logical statement, but it is specifically the infrequent-to-infrequent direction, working from smaller to larger itemsets, that Apriori actually exploits during its search, since that is what lets it stop expanding a branch of the search early.

blocks.text: 5. The Algorithm Step by Step

blocks.alt: Single items grow into pairs, then triples

blocks.text: Apriori proceeds in a level-wise fashion, working through itemsets one size at a time. In the first pass, it scans every transaction in the dataset and counts how often each individual item appears, keeping only the 1-itemsets that meet the minimum support threshold, the frequent 1-itemsets. In the second pass, it combines pairs of these surviving frequent 1-itemsets into candidate 2-itemsets, scans the transactions again to count how often each candidate 2-itemset actually appears together, and keeps only the ones that clear the threshold.

This process repeats, size by size: candidate 3-itemsets are built by combining surviving frequent 2-itemsets, counted, and filtered, and so on for 4-itemsets and beyond. At each new size, the Apriori Property is used to prune candidates before they are even counted, discarding any candidate itemset that contains a subset already known to be infrequent from an earlier pass. The algorithm stops once an entire pass produces no new frequent itemsets at all, at which point every frequent itemset, across every size, has been found.
6. Why Pruning Matters So Much

blocks.alt: Without pruning the search explodes combinatorially, with pruning it stays manageable

blocks.text: Without the Apriori Property's pruning, the number of candidate itemsets that would need to be checked grows combinatorially with the number of unique items in the dataset, an explosion that quickly becomes computationally infeasible even for a modestly sized product catalog with just a few hundred distinct items. A brute-force approach checking every possible combination of items simply does not scale.

By discarding any candidate itemset that contains even one infrequent subset before ever bothering to count it against the transaction data, Apriori dramatically reduces the number of itemsets that actually need to be checked at each pass. This pruning step, applying the Apriori Property directly during candidate generation rather than after the fact, is precisely what makes Apriori a practical, usable algorithm on real transaction datasets, rather than a purely theoretical exercise that would never finish running on data of any meaningful size.

blocks.text: 7. From Frequent Itemsets to Association Rules

blocks.alt: A frequent itemset splits into an if-then rule, becoming an association rule

blocks.text: Finding frequent itemsets is only the first half of Apriori's job. Once a frequent itemset is known, for instance discovering that bread, butter, and jam frequently appear together, the second half generates candidate association rules from it, statements of the form if a customer buys this, they are also likely to buy that. From the single itemset containing bread, butter, and jam, several different candidate rules can be generated: bread and butter implies jam, bread implies butter and jam, or butter and jam implies bread, among others.

Not every candidate rule generated this way turns out to be genuinely useful or reliable, however. Each candidate rule needs to be scored and filtered using dedicated metrics, specifically Support, Confidence, and Lift, each covered in full depth in their own dedicated topics immediately following this one and the next. These metrics distinguish a strong, actionable, trustworthy rule from a weak or misleading one, even when both rules are built from the same underlying frequent itemset.
8. Scalability Concerns

blocks.alt: A large item database makes Apriori run slowly

blocks.text: Apriori's level-wise design has a real practical cost: it requires one full pass over the entire transaction database for every single itemset size being considered, meaning finding frequent itemsets up to size five requires scanning the full dataset five separate times. On a transaction database with millions of records, each of these full scans is itself an expensive operation, and repeating it several times over compounds that cost substantially.

Beyond the repeated scanning cost, Apriori can also still generate a large number of candidate itemsets at each pass before the Apriori Property pruning has a chance to eliminate them, particularly in the earlier passes where fewer itemsets have yet been ruled out. These two costs together, repeated full database scans and potentially large candidate generation, are exactly what motivate FP-Growth, the very next topic in this module, an algorithm built specifically to find frequent itemsets while avoiding repeated full scans of the transaction database entirely.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: On genuinely large transaction datasets, with millions of transactions or a very large item catalog, plain Apriori's repeated full scans can become a real practical bottleneck, exactly the situation FP-Growth, covered next, was designed to address.

blocks.text: 9. Real-World Applications

Beyond its namesake retail setting, association rule mining built on Apriori-style frequent itemset discovery shows up across a wide range of practical domains. In retail, it directly informs decisions about which products to shelve near each other and which items to bundle together into promotional offers. In e-commerce, it powers the frequently-bought-together style recommendations shown alongside a product listing, surfacing items other customers have often purchased in the same order.

In web usage analysis, the same technique reveals which pages within a website tend to get visited together within the same browsing session, informing site navigation and content placement decisions. In healthcare, association rule mining has been applied to clinical records to discover which symptoms, conditions, or treatments tend to co-occur, surfacing patterns worth further clinical investigation. Across every one of these settings, the same core Apriori mechanics, frequent itemset discovery followed by rule generation and scoring, apply directly.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example
The example below runs Apriori on a small set of grocery transactions, finding frequent itemsets and generating candidate association rules from them.

code.content:
import pandas as pd
from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import apriori, association_rules
from mlxtend.preprocessing import TransactionEncoder

# Each inner list is one transaction, the set of items bought together
transactions = [
    ["bread", "butter", "jam"],
    ["bread", "butter"],
    ["bread", "milk"],
    ["bread", "butter", "jam", "milk"],
    ["butter", "jam"],
    ["bread", "butter", "milk"],
]

encoder = TransactionEncoder()
encoded_array = encoder.fit(transactions).transform(transactions)
df = pd.DataFrame(encoded_array, columns=encoder.columns_)

# Find frequent itemsets appearing in at least 40% of transactions
frequent_itemsets = apriori(df, min_support=0.4, use_colnames=True)
print("Frequent itemsets:")
print(frequent_itemsets)

# Generate association rules from those frequent itemsets
rules = association_rules(frequent_itemsets, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.6)
print("\nAssociation rules:")
print(rules[["antecedents", "consequents", "support", "confidence", "lift"]])

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: mlxtend's apriori function implements exactly the level-wise generate-count-filter cycle described in this topic, and association_rules then generates and scores candidate rules from the resulting frequent itemsets using the Support, Confidence, and Lift metrics covered in depth in the next few topics.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Association Rule Learning discovers which items tend to co-occur across transactions, a different unsupervised question from clustering.
Market Basket Analysis, discovering items frequently bought together, is Apriori's classic namesake application.
An itemset is frequent if it appears together across at least some minimum fraction of transactions.
The Apriori Property, anti-monotonicity, guarantees every subset of a frequent itemset is itself frequent, enabling aggressive pruning.
Apriori works level by level: generate candidates, count them against the data, filter by minimum support, repeat for the next size.
Pruning candidates whose subsets are already infrequent is what makes Apriori computationally practical on real data.
Frequent itemsets generate multiple candidate association rules, each needing to be scored by Support, Confidence, and Lift.
Requiring one full database scan per itemset size is a real scalability cost on very large transaction datasets.
Next up: FP-Growth, an algorithm that finds the same frequent itemsets while avoiding Apriori's repeated full database scans.
